summary.summary: {'summary': 'This report describes efficacy testing of a murine anti-lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) antibody (B3) and a humanized anti-LPA antibody (LT3114) in the collagen antibody–induced arthritis (CAIA) mouse model to assess reduction of arthritis-associated mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity. Prophylactic subcutaneous dosing (10 mg/kg, twice weekly, starting Day -8; n=6/group) with B3 or LT3114 prevented CAIA-induced mechanical and cold hypersensitivity but did not alter arthritis clinical scores. Therapeutic dosing (B3 10 or 40 mg/kg s.c., twice weekly, starting Day 12; n=6/group) showed that 10 mg/kg B3 reversed mechanical hypersensitivity beyond Day 39 and reversed heat hypersensitivity, whereas 40 mg/kg B3 and control IgG were ineffective. Mechanistic immunohistochemistry indicated that 10 mg/kg B3 reduced CAIA-induced up-regulation of α2δ1, P2X3 and galanin in dorsal root ganglia and prevented spinal astrocyte (GFAP) activation, but did not affect GAP43 up-regulation or microglial (Iba-1) activation. Overall, anti-LPA antibodies demonstrated activity against pain-like behaviors in both prophylactic and therapeutic paradigms at 10 mg/kg.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study objective and model', 'summary': 'Evaluate efficacy of murine (B3) and humanized (LT3114) anti-LPA antibodies to reduce mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity in male CBA mice using the collagen antibody–induced arthritis (CAIA) model (anti-collagen antibody cocktail on Day 0; 25 µg LPS i.p. on Day 5).'}, {'topic': 'Test articles, groups and dosing', 'summary': 'Test articles were murine anti-LPA (B3, Lot# HR101201), humanized anti-LPA (LT3114, Lot# LP101202) and control murine IgG2b (LT1015). Six groups (total 36 mice; n=6/group) were used. Prophylactic dosing: 10 mg/kg s.c. twice weekly starting Day -8. Therapeutic dosing: treatment from Day 12 with B3 at 10 or 40 mg/kg s.c. twice weekly; control arms received LT1015 or saline.'}, {'topic': 'Primary efficacy outcomes', 'summary': 'Prophylactic 10 mg/kg B3 or LT3114 prevented CAIA-induced mechanical and cold hypersensitivity at Day 14 without changing arthritis clinical score. Therapeutic 10 mg/kg B3 reversed mechanical hypersensitivity that persisted after resolution of inflammation (>Day 39) and reversed heat hypersensitivity; 40 mg/kg B3 and control IgG showed no efficacy.'}, {'topic': 'Behavioral assessments and timing', 'summary': 'Endpoints included tactile allodynia (von Frey, up-down method; baseline assessments Days -9 to -3), cold sensitivity (acetone drop scoring at Day 14 and inflammatory time points), and thermal (heat) nociception (Hargreaves apparatus; tested Day 17 and Day 41). Allodynia and clinical arthritis scores were measured at scheduled timepoints up to study end (Day 47).'}, {'topic': 'Mechanistic immunohistochemistry', 'summary': 'DRG immunostaining (galanin, P2X3, CACNA2D1/α2δ1, GAP43) showed that therapeutic B3 (10 mg/kg) attenuated CAIA-induced up-regulation of α2δ1, P2X3 and galanin but did not alter GAP43 up-regulation. In the spinal cord, B3 prevented CAIA-induced astrocyte (GFAP) activation but did not reverse microglial (Iba-1) activation.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusions', 'summary': 'Anti-LPA antibodies (B3 and LT3114) demonstrated analgesic efficacy in the CAIA model when dosed prophylactically or therapeutically at 10 mg/kg s.c., with associated normalization of several pain-related molecular markers in DRG and reduced spinal astrocyte activation. Efficacy was dose-dependent in the therapeutic paradigm, as a higher tested dose of B3 (40 mg/kg) lacked effect.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP wash-out primary pharmacodynamics study (Karolinska Institute) evaluated murine anti-LPA monoclonal antibody B3 (504B3) in the collagen antibody‑induced arthritis (CAIA) model in male CBA mice (6 groups, n=6/group). Arthritis was induced by IV anti-collagen antibody cocktail (1.5 mg/mouse) on Day 0 and boosted with LPS 25 µg i.p. on Day 5; animals received s.c. B3 (2 or 10 mg/kg) or control IgG twice weekly from Day 12–43 with wash-out and cross-over periods through Day 72. Mechanical hypersensitivity was measured by von Frey filaments (50% withdrawal threshold) and arthritis was scored visually (max 60/mouse). B3 at 10 mg/kg produced a significant, dose‑dependent reduction of tactile allodynia; 2 mg/kg showed partial efficacy and control antibody had no effect. Protection declined after treatment cessation in a manner consistent with antibody clearance, and delayed initiation of 10 mg/kg B3 (starting Day 57) reversed established allodynia to control levels within ~2 weeks.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study objective and setting', 'summary': 'Non‑GLP efficacy/wash‑out study at Karolinska Institute to test two doses of murine anti‑LPA mAb B3 (2 and 10 mg/kg), assess duration of protection after treatment cessation, and determine efficacy when treatment start was delayed until inflammation had resolved.'}, {'topic': 'Materials and study design', 'summary': 'Male CBA mice (six groups, n=6/group; total 36) underwent CAIA induction by IV anti‑collagen antibody cocktail (1.5 mg/mouse, Day 0) and LPS 25 µg i.p. (Day 5). Treatments (s.c.) were control IgG (LT1015, Lot# HR91184) or B3 (504B3, Lot# HR101201) twice weekly from Day 12 to 43; schedules included wash‑out (day 43 onward) and a cross‑over where saline animals were switched to B3 on Day 57. Mechanical thresholds and visual arthritis scoring were performed at scheduled time points through Day 72.'}, {'topic': 'Pharmacodynamic assessments', 'summary': 'Mechanical hypersensitivity was quantified using von Frey filaments with the up‑down method to calculate 50% withdrawal thresholds; arthritis severity was scored by inspection (digits 0–5, paw 0/5, ankle 0/5; max 15/leg, 60/mouse).'}, {'topic': 'Results', 'summary': 'B3 at 10 mg/kg produced a significant reduction in tactile allodynia and restored thresholds to levels indistinguishable from non‑arthritic controls after ~12 days of treatment; 2 mg/kg showed partial efficacy while control IgG had no effect. Upon cessation of 10 mg/kg dosing, protection waned consistent with expected antibody elimination; delayed treatment with 10 mg/kg beginning on Day 57 reversed established allodynia to control levels within ~2 weeks. A small, non‑specific effect on arthritis clinical score was noted at the lower dose.'}, {'topic': 'Data handling and statistics', 'summary': 'Data were summarized using descriptive statistics (mean, SD, SEM) and analyzed/graphically presented with GraphPad Prism v6.0; inferential testing used two‑way repeated measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post‑hoc comparisons as reported in the study.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusions', 'summary': 'Murine anti‑LPA mAb B3 produced dose‑dependent reductions in tactile hypersensitivity in the CAIA model, with effects persisting after treatment consistent with antibody kinetics, and was effective when therapy was delayed until after inflammation resolved.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP study evaluated the efficacy of murine (B3) and humanized (LT3114) anti-lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) monoclonal antibodies in a rat model of acute peripheral inflammatory pain induced by intraplantar λ-carrageenan. summary.summary: {'summary': 'A Porsolt tail‑flick study in male NMRI mice evaluated analgesic activity after s.c. administration of 1023 (50 mg/kg) and 3114 (10 and 50 mg/kg) given on Day 0 (24 h before testing). Tail‑flick latency was measured at baseline, Day 1 and Day 3; morphine (8 mg/kg s.c., 30 min prior) was used as reference. Neither 1023 nor 3114 produced statistically significant increases in withdrawal latency versus vehicle, although dose‑dependent tendencies to increase latency were observed on Day 3 (+54% for 1023; +41% and +68% for 3114 10 and 50 mg/kg, respectively). Vehicle group results (decreased latency versus neutral PBS control) complicate interpretation; morphine produced robust, statistically significant analgesia (+89% Day 1, +71% Day 3, p < 0.001). Complementary two‑way ANOVA showed a significant treatment effect (p = 0.0002) but post‑hoc multiple comparisons did not show significant differences between test articles and controls.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study design and objective', 'summary': 'Aim: assess potential analgesic effects of 1023 and 3114 using the tail‑flick assay. Male NMRI mice (10 per group) received test articles s.c. on Day 0 (24 h before first test); assessments were at baseline, Day 1 and Day 3. Morphine 8 mg/kg s.c. (30 min prior) served as reference.'}, {'topic': 'Dosing and groups', 'summary': 'Groups: neutral vehicle (PBS), vehicle (formulation buffer), 1023 at 50 mg/kg, 3114 at 10 and 50 mg/kg, and morphine 8 mg/kg. Administration volume was 10 mL/kg; ten animals per group.'}, {'topic': 'Efficacy results', 'summary': '1023 (50 mg/kg) and 3114 (10 and 50 mg/kg) did not produce statistically significant increases in tail‑flick latency versus vehicle. Observed mean percent changes on Day 3 were +54% (1023), +41% (3114 10 mg/kg) and +68% (3114 50 mg/kg), but these were not significant. Vehicle tended to show decreased latencies versus neutral PBS (≈‑20% Day 1, ≈‑34% Day 3), confounding interpretation.'}, {'topic': 'Reference control performance', 'summary': 'Morphine produced marked and statistically significant analgesia: Day 1 mean latency 14.4 ± 0.4 s (+89%, p < 0.001) and Day 3 mean latency 14.5 ± 0.3 s (+71%, p < 0.001), confirming assay sensitivity.'}, {'topic': 'Statistical analysis and interpretation', 'summary': 'Primary analyses used one‑way ANOVA with Dunnett’s test (and unpaired t tests for reference); complementary two‑way RM ANOVA (treatment and time) found a significant treatment effect (F (2,27) = 11.65, p = 0.0002) while interaction and time were not significant. Post‑hoc Bonferroni comparisons between test articles and controls were not statistically significant.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusion', 'summary': 'The study concludes absence of statistically significant analgesic activity for 1023 (50 mg/kg) and 3114 (10 and 50 mg/kg) after s.c. administration in the tail‑flick test; Day 3 tendencies toward increased latency were observed but are complicated by vehicle effects.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'A GLP nonclinical efficacy study (Study No. 14.0061; LT3114-PHA-008-R) evaluated test substances 1015 (30 mg/kg i.v.) and murine antibody B3 (10 and 30 mg/kg i.v.) in the rat spinal nerve ligation (Chung) neuropathic pain model. Rats (10/group) were dosed on Days 14, 17, 21 and 24 post‑surgery and assessed by electronic von Frey (tactile allodynia) and plantar (thermal hyperalgesia) tests; morphine (12 mg/kg i.p.) and gabapentin (100 mg/kg i.p.) were included as reference/comparator agents. By the prespecified one‑way ANOVA (with Dunnett’s post hoc) there were no statistically significant analgesic effects of 1015 (30 mg/kg) or B3 (10 and 30 mg/kg) versus vehicle across testing days, although secondary unpaired t‑tests and sponsor complementary analyses identified transient, test‑specific effects. Notably, B3 (30 mg/kg) produced significant increases in thermal paw‑withdrawal latency at early tests and B3 (10 mg/kg) showed a significant effect at a later test; morphine and gabapentin produced expected analgesic responses. Plasma concentrations of B3 were measured by ELISA at termination and were detectable in B3‑treated animals (measured ranges: ~60.6–432.8 µg/mL for 10 mg/kg group, ~50.3–1106.1 µg/mL for 30 mg/kg group), while concentrations in vehicle, 1015 and reference/comparator groups were reported as 0.00 µg/mL.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study design and methods', 'summary': 'Male Sprague–Dawley rats (10 per group) underwent L5 spinal nerve ligation and were tested pre‑surgery, pre‑dosing (Days 11–13) and 3 days after each i.v. dose (Days 17, 21, 24 and 27). Test articles: 1015 (30 mg/kg i.v., single dose level) and B3 (10 and 30 mg/kg i.v.); dosing on Days 14, 17, 21 and 24. Reference/comparator: morphine 12 mg/kg i.p. (30 min pretest on Day 14) and gabapentin 100 mg/kg i.p. (180 min pretest on Day 21). Primary endpoints were tactile allodynia (electronic von Frey) and thermal hyperalgesia (plantar test); primary statistics were one‑way ANOVA with Dunnett’s post hoc, supplemented by unpaired Student’s t tests and sponsor two‑way ANOVA.'}, {'topic': 'Tactile (electronic von Frey) results', 'summary': 'Baseline on Day 14 confirmed tactile allodynia in lesioned paws vs non‑lesioned paws (≈‑86% to ‑89%, p<0.001). One‑way ANOVA on delta from baseline revealed no significant group effects of 1015 or B3 at the scheduled test days. Secondary unpaired t‑tests noted small, transient increases in force required for paw withdrawal after the first administration for 1015 (30 mg/kg) and B3 (30 mg/kg), but these were not sustained across all tests.'}, {'topic': 'Thermal (plantar) results', 'summary': 'Baseline on Day 14 confirmed thermal hyperalgesia in lesioned paws vs non‑lesioned paws (≈‑43% to ‑57%, p<0.001). By primary ANOVA there were no significant effects of 1015 or B3 across scheduled testing days. Complementary analyses identified that B3 (30 mg/kg) significantly increased paw‑withdrawal latency (thermal) at early post‑dose tests (Test 1 and Test 2) and B3 (10 mg/kg) showed a significant increase at Test 3; 1015 showed a non‑significant trend in some comparisons. Morphine increased paw‑withdrawal latency and gabapentin increased tactile thresholds as expected.'}, {'topic': 'Statistical analyses and sponsor assessment', 'summary': 'Primary analysis used one‑way ANOVA with Dunnett’s post hoc; additional unpaired Student’s t tests were applied to explore apparent increases. The sponsor performed complementary two‑way ANOVA and Bonferroni multiple comparisons; these supplementary analyses identified several significant pairwise differences (noted as transient and test‑specific), but the overall study conclusion reported absence of significant analgesia for 1015 and B3 when assessed by the primary ANOVA.'}, {'topic': 'Pharmacokinetic / exposure data', 'summary': 'Plasma concentrations of B3 were measured at termination by ELISA (Appendix 1). B3 was undetectable (0.00 µg/mL) in vehicle, 1015, morphine and gabapentin groups; measurable concentrations were reported in B3‑treated animals. Observed B3 concentrations in the 10 mg/kg group included values up to ~432.82 µg/mL (with one 0.00 reported), and in the 30 mg/kg group up to ~1106.06 µg/mL, demonstrating systemic exposure at the time of sampling.'}, {'topic': 'Overall conclusion', 'summary': 'Under the study conditions, 1015 (30 mg/kg i.v.) and B3 (10 and 30 mg/kg i.v.) did not demonstrate statistically significant analgesic effects versus vehicle by the prespecified ANOVA across repeated dosing in the Chung/SNL rat model. Supplementary analyses revealed transient, dose‑ and test‑dependent signals for B3 (notably in thermal assays) and isolated tactile responses for both test articles after the first administration; these were not consistent across all time points. Positive control agents (morphine, gabapentin) produced expected analgesic responses, supporting model sensitivity.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'A GLP-like efficacy study in male Sprague-Dawley rats with streptozocin (55 mg/kg IV)–induced diabetes evaluated twice-weekly IV dosing of antibodies for reversal of diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN). Treatments (administered starting five weeks after STZ) included vehicle (PBS), LT1015 (control IgG2b, 30 mg/kg), 504B3 (murine anti‑LPA, 10 and 30 mg/kg) and LT3114 (human anti‑LPA, 30 mg/kg); endpoints were thermal sensitivity (Hargreaves) and mechanical sensitivity (von Frey/paw withdrawal pressure). LT3114 (30 mg/kg) produced significant analgesic effects (increased thermal latency and increased withdrawal pressure) after one week of treatment and sustained effects on mechanical and thermal endpoints; 504B3 showed a transient amelioration of DPN at the highest dose (30 mg/kg). LT1015 (30 mg/kg) had no therapeutic effect; gabapentin (30 mg/kg SC, single dose on Day 59) increased mechanical withdrawal thresholds but not thermal latency. Plasma antibody concentrations were measured by ELISA and confirmed systemic exposure (e.g., LT3114: 135–627 µg/mL).', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study design and model', 'summary': 'Male Sprague-Dawley rats received 55 mg/kg streptozocin IV to induce diabetes (blood glucose >300 mg/dL by Day 7). Animals were randomized by left-paw Hargreaves response and body weight; dosing (IV, 5 mL/kg) of vehicle or antibodies was initiated five weeks after STZ and given twice weekly for four weeks. Primary endpoints were thermal latency (Hargreaves) and mechanical paw withdrawal pressure (von Frey), assessed weekly.'}, {'topic': 'Treatments and dosing groups', 'summary': 'Groups included non-diseased PBS, diseased PBS, LT1015 (30 mg/kg), 504B3 (10 and 30 mg/kg), and LT3114 (30 mg/kg). Fresh dosing solutions were prepared twice weekly and animals monitored for weight, clinical signs, and mortality; several animals were found dead during the study (noted in records).'}, {'topic': 'Efficacy — thermal and mechanical endpoints', 'summary': 'LT3114 (30 mg/kg) produced statistically significant increases in pain latency (Hargreaves) and increased paw withdrawal pressures, with effects apparent after the first week of treatment. 504B3 showed a transient improvement of DPN at the 30 mg/kg dose starting at week 7. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP, preliminary rat study (LT3114-PHA-012-R) evaluated the pharmacodynamic efficacy of a murine anti-S1P antibody (LT1002) and an anti-LPA antibody (504B3) versus their isotype controls (LT1017, LT1015) in a paclitaxel (1 mg/kg i.p., D0, D2, D4, D6)-induced neuropathic pain model. Antibodies were administered i.v. at 25 mg/kg one day before the first paclitaxel injection and on days 2, 5, 8, 11 and 14; mechanical withdrawal thresholds were measured by electronic von Frey. Paclitaxel induced significant bilateral mechanical allodynia versus vehicle; treatment with LT1002 or 504B3 significantly attenuated mechano-allodynia at day 16 while isotype controls had no effect. Group size was n=3 animals and data were analyzed by two-tailed two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc comparisons; animal body weights showed no differences between groups.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study overview and objective', 'summary': 'Pharmacological assessment of murine anti-S1P (LT1002) and anti-LPA (504B3) antibodies to determine whether they ameliorate paclitaxel-induced neuropathic pain in rats; study performed as a preliminary, non-GLP investigation (Report LT3114-PHA-012-R).'}, {'topic': 'Experimental design and dosing', 'summary': 'Male Sprague Dawley rats (200–210 g) received paclitaxel 1 mg/kg i.p. on D0, D2, D4 and D6 (cumulative 4 mg/kg) or vehicle; test antibodies (LT1002, 504B3) and isotype controls (LT1017, LT1015) were given i.v. at 25 mg/kg one day prior to the first paclitaxel dose and on days 2, 5, 8, 11 and 14.'}, {'topic': 'Pharmacodynamic assessments', 'summary': 'Primary endpoint was mechanical paw-withdrawal threshold measured using an electronic von Frey (dynamic plantar aesthesiometer) at D-1, D0 and subsequently on D12 and D16; thresholds were averaged across both hind paws and reported as mean ± SEM.'}, {'topic': 'Results and statistical analysis', 'summary': 'Paclitaxel produced time-dependent bilateral mechano-allodynia versus vehicle; LT1002 and 504B3 each significantly attenuated mechano-allodynia at day 16 while isotype controls (LT1017, LT1015) did not. section_sources.summary_text: {"summary": "{'summary': 'This non-GLP, preliminary rat study (LT3114-PHA-012-R) evaluated the pharmacodynamic efficacy of a murine anti-S1P antibody (LT1002) and an anti-LPA antibody (504B3) versus their isotype controls (LT1017, LT1015) in a paclitaxel (1 mg/kg i.p., D0, D2, D4, D6)-induced neuropathic pain model. Antibodies were administered i.v. at 25 mg/kg one day before the first paclitaxel injection and on days 2, 5, 8, 11 and 14; mechanical withdrawal thresholds were measured by electronic von Frey. Paclitaxel induced significant bilateral mechanical allodynia versus vehicle; treatment with LT1002 or 504B3 significantly attenuated mechano-allodynia at day 16 while isotype controls had no effect. Group size was n=3 animals and data were analyzed by two-tailed two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc comparisons; animal body weights showed no differences between groups.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study overview and objective', 'summary': 'Pharmacological assessment of murine anti-S1P (LT1002) and anti-LPA (504B3) antibodies to determine whether they ameliorate paclitaxel-induced neuropathic pain in rats; study performed as a preliminary, non-GLP investigation (Report LT3114-PHA-012-R).'}, {'topic': 'Experimental design and dosing', 'summary': 'Male Sprague Dawley rats (200–210 g) received paclitaxel 1 mg/kg i.p. on D0, D2, D4 and D6 (cumulative 4 mg/kg) or vehicle; test antibodies (LT1002, 504B3) and isotype controls (LT1017, LT1015) were given i.v. at 25 mg/kg one day prior to the first paclitaxel dose and on days 2, 5, 8, 11 and 14.'}, {'topic': 'Pharmacodynamic assessments', 'summary': 'Primary endpoint was mechanical paw-withdrawal threshold measured using an electronic von Frey (dynamic plantar aesthesiometer) at D-1, D0 and subsequently on D12 and D16; thresholds were averaged across both hind paws and reported as mean ± SEM.'}, {'topic': 'Results and statistical analysis', 'summary': 'Paclitaxel produced time-dependent bilateral mechano-allodynia versus vehicle; LT1002 and 504B3 each significantly attenuated mechano-allodynia at day 16 while isotype controls (LT1017, LT1015) did not. Data (n=3/group) were analyzed by two-tailed, two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc comparisons to the paclitaxel group; significance indicators and thresholds are reported in the study.'}, {'topic': 'Additional observations and limitations', 'summary': 'Animal body weights were recorded (Table 1) with no differences across groups. The study is preliminary with small group size (n=3) and conducted non-GLP, which should be considered when interpreting findings.'}]}", "keywords": ["anti-S1P (LT1002)", "anti-LPA (504B3)", "paclitaxel 1 mg/kg", "mechanical allodynia", "von Frey", "Sprague Dawley rats", "isotype controls", "25 mg/kg i.v.", "two-way ANOVA", "non-GLP"]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP in vivo study evaluated the efficacy of a murine anti-LPA monoclonal antibody (B3) in male DBA/2 mice with paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy. Paclitaxel (1 mg/kg i.p. on days 1, 3, 5 and 7; cumulative 4 mg/kg) produced tactile allodynia measured by von Frey paw withdrawal thresholds; B3 (30 mg/kg s.c., initiated day 3, twice weekly) produced a significant, sustained reversal of allodynia in the early phase (p < 0.001) and also reversed allodynia when dosed in the late phase (p < 0.05). B3 treatment significantly reduced circulating bioactive LPA as measured by an EDG2 (LPA1) β-arrestin reporter assay (p < 0.0001). Terminal plasma antibody concentrations were consistent with dosing (group mean 282.55 µg/mL for mice switched to B3; mean 13.41 µg/mL for mice switched from B3 to control), and no treatment-related body weight differences were observed.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study objective and design', 'summary': 'Objective was to test whether murine anti-LPA mAb B3 attenuates pain behavior in a paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy model in male DBA/2 mice. Paclitaxel was given i.p. at 1 mg/kg on days 1, 3, 5 and 7 (cumulative 4 mg/kg); B3 or control IgG (1014) were dosed s.c. at 30 mg/kg beginning day 3 and twice weekly, with a crossover at day 21 to evaluate late-phase/post-treatment effects. Gabapentin (100 mg/kg i.p.) and PBS were included as reference controls.'}, {'topic': 'Methods and assays', 'summary': 'Tactile paw withdrawal thresholds (PWT) were measured bilaterally using calibrated von Frey filaments and the up-down Dixon method by a blinded observer. Plasma B3 concentrations were quantified by a direct-binding ELISA; bioactive LPA was measured using a CHO-K1 EDG2 (LPA receptor) β-arrestin PathHunter reporter assay. Data were analyzed with repeated-measures two-way ANOVA for behavioral endpoints and one-way ANOVA for biochemical measures with Bonferroni post-hoc tests.'}, {'topic': 'Behavioral efficacy (mechanical allodynia)', 'summary': 'Paclitaxel induced robust mechanical allodynia by day 3. Subcutaneous B3 (30 mg/kg) produced a significant, sustained reversal of tactile allodynia in the early phase (p < 0.001) and reversed established allodynia when started in the late phase (p < 0.05); switching from B3 to control IgG led to return of allodynia after two doses. Gabapentin significantly attenuated allodynia in both early and late phases (p < 0.0001), with greater apparent potency in the early phase.'}, {'topic': 'Biomarker: bioactive LPA', 'summary': 'Plasma levels of bioactive LPA (able to activate LPA1 in the reporter assay) showed no change with paclitaxel versus vehicle, whereas B3 treatment significantly reduced circulating bioactive LPA (Figure 3; p < 0.0001 by one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction).'}, {'topic': 'Antibody concentrations at takedown', 'summary': "Terminal plasma B3 concentrations measured by direct ELISA were reported per animal (Table 3). Group mean [B3] was 282.55 µg/mL for the 'Paclitaxel + 1014 switch to B3' group and 13.41 µg/mL for the 'Paclitaxel + B3 switch to 1014' group; several individual values in the latter group were noted as below the standard linear range."}, {'topic': 'General tolerability / body weight', 'summary': 'Body weight monitoring (2–3 times/week) showed no significant differences between vehicle and paclitaxel-treated groups receiving PBS, gabapentin, 1014 or B3 according to the study schedule.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'A non-GLP competition ELISA assessed cross-reactivity of murine (504B3/B3) and humanized anti-LPA monoclonal antibodies (LT3015, LT3017, LT3114) against a panel of lipids structurally related to lysophosphatidic acid (LPA). Plates were coated with 18:0 LPA (0.33 µg/mL) and antibodies (0.5 µg/mL) were pre-incubated with test lipids at concentrations up to 5 µM before measurement (TMB, read 450 nm). At 2.5 µM, strong competition was observed only with LPA species (LPA 18:2: LT3015 44%, LT3017 47%, LT3114 61%, B3 71%; LPA C18:1: 12–30% across antibodies), while the remaining tested lipids produced minimal percent inhibition. The report concludes there is no significant cross-reactivity with non-LPA lipids up to 5 µM, supporting the specificity of the anti-LPA antibodies for LPA.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study objective', 'summary': 'Evaluate potential binding (cross-reactivity) of murine and humanized anti-LPA monoclonal antibodies to a panel of lipids structurally/chemically similar to LPA.'}, {'topic': 'Materials and test articles', 'summary': 'Test articles included humanized antibodies LT3015, LT3017, LT3114 and murine 504B3/B3; a lipid panel (Table 1) comprised multiple LPA species and related lipids (e.g., S1P, sphingosine, LPC, LPE, LPG, LPS, Lyso PI, PS, PC, PG, PA, PE, PAF, cyclic LPA, BrP-LPA, 2-AG, LBPA, DAG, glycerol phosphate).'}, {'topic': 'Methods (assay)', 'summary': 'Specificity was determined by competition ELISA with plates coated with 18:0 LPA (0.33 µg/mL); antibodies were diluted to 0.5 µg/mL and pre-incubated with lipids at 5, 2.5, 1.25, 0.625 and 0 µM (lipid:antibody 3:1), followed by HRP-conjugated secondary detection (1:20,000), TMB development (8 min), stop with 1 M H2SO4 and OD measurement at 450 nm; competition curves were analyzed and percent inhibition at 2.5 µM calculated.'}, {'topic': 'Results', 'summary': 'Competition data (Table 3) show pronounced inhibition only for LPA species (LPA 18:2: LT3015 44%, LT3017 47%, LT3114 61%, B3 71%; LPA C18:1: LT3015 12%, LT3017 12%, LT3114 20%, B3 30%). Non-LPA lipids produced minimal percent inhibition at 2.5 µM (generally near 0% with occasional low single-digit values), indicating negligible competition for plated 18:0 LPA.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusions and data archive', 'summary': 'Authors conclude there is no significant cross-reactivity of the tested anti-LPA antibodies with non-LPA lipids up to 5 µM, with the exception of LPA species. Raw data and notebooks are archived (Lpath Notebooks #181, ELISA Binder #5, Tab 181; electronic path provided in report).'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP study evaluated binding of a murine anti-LPA monoclonal antibody (B3) and a humanized variant (LT3114) to physiologically relevant LPA isoforms using direct and competition ELISA formats. Direct ELISA produced comparable binding curves with EC50 values of 33.5 ng/mL (B3) and 24.4 ng/mL (LT3114). Competition assays measured affinities (Ki) across native LPA species (16:0, 18:0, 18:1, 18:2, 20:4), with reported Ki values ranging approximately 15.8 nM to 986 nM and specific examples of ~16 nM for 18:2 and ~360 nM for 18:1. Data were analyzed with GraphPad/Excel and Ki values calculated using the Cheng-Prusoff equation. The report concludes the antibodies are potent and bind a wide range of physiologically relevant LPA isoforms.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study overview', 'summary': 'Non-GLP binding study comparing murine (B3) and humanized (LT3114) monoclonal antibodies to LPA; objective was to demonstrate sensitivity and specificity for acyl-chain LPA isoforms.'}, {'topic': 'Materials and test articles', 'summary': 'Test articles were murine anti-LPA antibody 504B3 (B3, Lot # HR121456) and humanized LT3114 (Lot # LP121425); assays used C12-LPA-BSA capture and biotinylated LPA competitors.'}, {'topic': 'Assay methods', 'summary': 'Both direct binding ELISA (C12-LPA-BSA coated plates, TMB detection, read at 450 nm) and competition ELISA (antibody capture, LPA-biotin competitor, SA-HRP detection) were developed to assess binding and specificity.'}, {'topic': 'Results and affinity', 'summary': 'Direct ELISA EC50s were 33.5 ng/mL (B3) and 24.4 ng/mL (LT3114). Competition ELISA yielded Ki values across 16:0, 18:0, 18:1, 18:2, and 20:4 LPA; reported range ~15.8 nM to 986 nM with examples of ~16 nM for 18:2 and ~360 nM for 18:1.'}, {'topic': 'Data analysis and calculations', 'summary': 'Raw readings were recorded on a Thermo Multiskan EX and analyzed with GraphPad Prism and Excel; Ki values were derived using the Cheng-Prusoff equation and antibody Kd from separate saturation binding experiments.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusion and archive', 'summary': 'The report concludes B3 and LT3114 are potent, specific neutralizing antibodies that bind a broad set of physiologically relevant LPA isoforms. Supporting raw data are archived in Lpath notebooks (#312, #301, #220).'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'A cell-based PathHunter β-arrestin complementation assay in CHO-K1 EDG2/4/7 cells was developed to evaluate LPA isoform binding to LPA receptors and to measure inhibition of receptor activation by anti-LPA antibodies. LPA isoforms tested included 16:0, 18:0, 18:1-alkyl, 18:1-acyl, 18:2 and 20:4; all showed higher affinity for LPAR1 than for LPAR2/3. Both the murine antibody 504B3 (B3, Lot HR101201) and the humanized antibody LT3114 (Lot LP011202) produced dose-dependent inhibition of LPA binding to LPAR1 and prevented receptor activation with similar whole-cell activity. Key assay parameters included plating 20,000 cells/well, LPA titration for binding curves (text reports 0–3 mM; figure legend reports 0–30 µM), inhibition experiments using 200 nM LPA for 18:1/18:2 or 10 mM LPA for 18:0/20:4 with antibodies at 0–1.5 mg/mL, chemiluminescent detection, and data fitting with GraphPad Prism 5 (four-parameter fit).', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study objective and design', 'summary': 'Developed a cell-based assay to assess LPA receptor activation by multiple LPA isoforms and to evaluate inhibition of signaling by anti-LPA antibodies using DiscoveRx PathHunter β-arrestin complementation.'}, {'topic': 'Test articles', 'summary': 'Murine anti-LPA antibody 504B3 (B3, Lot HR101201) and humanized anti-LPA antibody LT3114 (Lot LP011202) were evaluated for inhibition of LPA binding and receptor activation.'}, {'topic': 'Cells and assay methodology', 'summary': 'CHO-K1 EDG2 (LPAR1), EDG4 (LPAR2) and EDG7 (LPAR3) PathHunter clones were expanded and plated at 20,000 cells/well; plates were serum-starved, treated with titrated LPA isoforms, and detected by chemiluminescence using Cell Assay Buffer/Emerald II/Galacton Star (19:5:1).'}, {'topic': 'Key experimental conditions', 'summary': 'LPA binding curves were prepared by titration (text reports 0–3 mM; figure legend reports 0–30 µM). In inhibition assays, 200 nM LPA was used for 18:1 and 18:2, 10 mM LPA for 18:0 and 20:4, and antibody concentrations ranged 0–1.5 mg/mL; plates were read on a luminescence reader.'}, {'topic': 'Results and data analysis', 'summary': 'All tested LPA isoforms showed higher affinity for LPAR1 versus LPAR2/3; B3 and LT3114 produced dose-dependent inhibition of LPA binding to LPAR1 with similar whole-cell activity. Data were analyzed with GraphPad Prism 5 using a four-parameter fit.'}, {'topic': 'Data archive', 'summary': 'Primary raw data are archived in Lpath Notebook #210 (pp. 24–27; 59; 122–125).'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'Non-GLP Lpath study LT3114-PHA-018-R assessed the efficacy of IV anti-LPA antibody 504B3 (and antibody control LT1015) in the Brennan post‑incisional pain model in Sprague Dawley rats. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This non-GLP pharmacology study evaluated lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) levels in a streptozotocin (STZ) rat model of insulin-deficient diabetes and tested preliminary efficacy of an anti-LPA antibody (murine B3; humanized lead LT3114). Diabetic rats developed tactile allodynia and showed elevated plasma LPA by LC-MS and increased LPA immunostaining in dorsal root ganglia versus non-diabetic controls. A single combined IV (10 mg/kg) and intrathecal (10 μg) dose of B3 reduced bioactive/total plasma LPA, restored plasma LPA toward control levels, and increased paw withdrawal threshold versus isotype control or vehicle. Residual free plasma LPA (estimated by KinExA) inversely correlated with behavioral efficacy. Analyses were descriptive and by ANOVA; primary assays included LC-MS, a cell-based LPAR1 reporter assay, immunohistochemistry, and KinExA.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study objective and design', 'summary': 'Purpose was to determine whether LPA is upregulated in STZ-induced diabetic rats and to assess preliminary efficacy of an anti-LPA antibody. Mass spectrometry was performed by Dr. Yan Xu; other assays were run at Lpath.'}, {'topic': 'Immunohistochemistry findings', 'summary': 'Frozen DRG sections (5 μm) stained with a humanized anti-LPA antibody (LT3211) showed increased LPA immunoreactivity in medium and small ganglion cell bodies of STZ rats compared with controls. summary.summary: {'summary': 'This GLP safety pharmacology study evaluated cardiovascular and thermoregulatory effects of LT3114 after a single ~3-minute slow IV bolus in telemetry-instrumented male Cynomolgus monkeys. A crossover design (n=8) compared vehicle and LT3114 at target doses of 10 and 50 mg/kg with continuous telemetry (in-box ~0–120 min; in-cage ~3–24 h) and periodic ECG waveform tracings. Systolic, diastolic and mean arterial pressures, and most heart rate and ECG intervals (PR, QRS, QT) showed no test article–related effects; an acute heart rate increase (~100 bpm) in one animal during dosing (needle displacement/re-handling) produced large variability and an artifactual QTcB trend. Sporadic small in-cage body temperature changes (max 0.7°C) and no test-article–related clinical observations or body weight effects were noted. Plasma TK confirmed exposure with a dose response; the 50 mg/kg dose was considered the NOAEL for this study.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study design and compliance', 'summary': 'GLP study conducted at Battelle using eight male Cynomolgus monkeys surgically implanted with radiotelemetry transmitters in a crossover design; animals received vehicle (Day 1) and LT3114 (10 and 50 mg/kg, Day 4) via ~3-minute slow IV bolus at 2 mL/kg.'}, {'topic': 'Telemetry and ECG assessment', 'summary': 'Continuous telemetry collected systolic/diastolic/mean arterial pressures, heart rate, core body temperature and ECG (averaged per 5-min intervals) with periodic ~60-second ECG tracings at prespecified post-dose times; QT was corrected using Bazett’s formula (QTcB).'}, {'topic': 'Cardiovascular results', 'summary': 'Group mean systolic, diastolic and mean blood pressures were not remarkably different from vehicle in both in-box and in-cage data; heart rate and ECG intervals (PR, QRS, QT) showed no test-article–related changes overall. One animal (203) experienced a dosing-related acute heart rate increase (~100 BPM) due to needle displacement and re-handling, which increased variability and caused an apparent QTcB artifact (overcorrection) in the 50 mg/kg group.'}, {'topic': 'Body temperature, clinical observations and body weight', 'summary': 'In-cage body temperature showed sporadic small increases/decreases between 3.5 and 24 h post-dose (maximum change 0.7°C) that were not considered physiologically relevant or related to LT3114. There were no test-article–related clinical observations or body weight changes.'}, {'topic': 'Dose formulation analysis and toxicokinetics', 'summary': 'Formulation concentration and homogeneity were assessed (report in Appendix B); TK analysis by validated ELISA (Appendix G) showed dose-related plasma exposure, confirming systemic exposure following IV administration.'}, {'topic': 'Conclusion / NOAEL', 'summary': 'No adverse cardiovascular, ECG, thermoregulatory, clinical or body weight effects attributable to LT3114 were identified up to 50 mg/kg; 50 mg/kg was considered the NOAEL for this study.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'A GLP-compliant, AAALAC-accredited telemetry study evaluated cardiovascular safety of LT3114 after a single ~3-minute slow IV bolus (2 mL/kg) in male cynomolgus monkeys (n=8) using a crossover design (vehicle Day 1; LT3114 Day 4 at target 10 and 50 mg/kg). Continuous telemetry (in-box ~0–120 min and in-cage ~3–24 h) captured systolic/diastolic/mean arterial pressure, heart rate, core body temperature and ECG (PR, QRS, QT, QTcB); additional clinical observations, body weights, and plasma TK (ELISA) were measured. No test-article–related, biologically meaningful changes in blood pressure, heart rate, PR, QRS or QT were observed; an isolated large heart-rate increase in Animal 203 was attributed to a dosing complication and caused transient QTcB overcorrection by Bazett’s formula. Sporadic, small in-cage body temperature changes (≤0.7°C) and no clinical signs or body weight effects were considered not test-article–related. TK confirmed dose-related exposure; the 50 mg/kg dose was considered the NOAEL in this study.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study design and dosing', 'summary': 'Eight male cynomolgus monkeys (one replacement animal excluded prior to study) underwent a crossover protocol with vehicle (Day 1) and LT3114 (Day 4) administered as an approximate 3-minute slow IV bolus at target doses of 0, 10, and 50 mg/kg in a volume of 2 mL/kg. Animals were surgically implanted with radiotelemetry transmitters prior to dosing.'}, {'topic': 'Telemetry and endpoints', 'summary': 'Continuous Dataquest A.R.T. telemetry acquired systemic arterial pressures (systolic, diastolic, mean), heart rate, core body temperature and ECG intervals (PR, QRS, QT, RR) in isolation boxes (in-box) and home cages (in-cage). Periodic 60-second ECG tracings were also recorded and qualitatively reviewed by the Study Cardiologist.'}, {'topic': 'Cardiovascular and ECG results', 'summary': 'Group mean blood pressures and heart rate showed no remarkable differences from vehicle. ECG intervals PR, QRS and QT were not markedly different from vehicle; a transient increasing trend in QTcB at 20–50 minutes in the 50 mg/kg group was attributed to a dosing-related heart-rate increase in Animal 203 and to Bazett overcorrection, and was not considered test-article–related.'}, {'topic': 'Body temperature, clinical observations and body weight', 'summary': 'In-cage body temperature showed sporadic small increases and decreases between 3.5 and 24 hours post-dose (maximum change reported 0.7°C) that were not considered physiologically relevant or attributable to LT3114. There were no test-article–related clinical observations or changes in body weight.'}, {'topic': 'Toxicokinetics and bioanalysis', 'summary': 'Plasma concentrations of LT3114 were measured by a validated ELISA (BQL = 100 ng/mL). TK demonstrated a dose-response relationship and confirmed exposure at the tested dose levels; individual animal concentration data and the bioanalytical report are provided in Appendix G.'}, {'topic': 'Statistics, QA and regulatory compliance', 'summary': 'Telemetry data were baseline-adjusted and analyzed using repeated-measures mixed-effects ANOVA with control of multiplicity (Benjamini–Hochberg across intervals and Bonferroni for pairwise comparisons to vehicle). The study was conducted under FDA GLP (21 CFR Part 58) at an AAALAC-accredited facility and inspected by the Quality Assurance Unit; QA audits and appendices with raw and statistical data are included.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'This GLP-style safety pharmacology study evaluated LT3114 in female C57BL/6 mice (n=8/group, 10–11 weeks) using two subcutaneous dose levels (10 and 50 mg/kg) administered on Days 1, 4, 8 and 11 to assess wound healing (percent wound closure AUC and terminal tensile strength). Both 10 and 50 mg/kg produced statistically significant acceleration of wound closure versus vehicle (reported p<0.0006 and p<0.0101, respectively) but neither dose altered tensile (breaking) strength at Day 14. All treated animals had quantifiable plasma LT3114 by two ELISA methods (direct human IgG and antigen-laid down), the methods gave generally similar results and no clear dose response between 10 and 50 mg/kg was observed. All animals survived to scheduled termination with no test-article related clinical observations or body weight changes; a single protocol deviation (late 1-hr postdose observation on Day 4) was reported and judged not to affect study integrity. The report notes that the apparent effect on early wound closure may reflect modulation of the inflammatory phase and recommends histological evaluation to confirm effects on inflammation/remodeling.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study design and test system', 'summary': 'Female C57BL/6 mice (8 per group, 10–11 weeks) received subcutaneous dosing of vehicle, 10 mg/kg or 50 mg/kg LT3114 on Days 1, 4, 8 and 11 following creation of cranial (6 mm punch) and caudal (1 cm linear) wounds; the cranial wound was used for quantitative assessment and terminal tensile testing on Day 14.'}, {'topic': 'Dosing, procedures and sample collection', 'summary': 'LT3114 (GA121459, 32.1 mg/mL) was dosed SC with procedures including analgesia and semi‑occlusive dressing; body weights and wound photographs were taken at prespecified intervals and blood for plasma PK was collected at necropsy (cardiac puncture, K3-EDTA).'}, {'topic': 'Efficacy endpoints and results', 'summary': 'Percent wound closure was measured on Days 3, 6, 9, 13 and 14 and summarized as AUC; both 10 and 50 mg/kg LT3114 significantly accelerated wound closure versus vehicle (reported p-values p<0.0006 and p<0.0101), while terminal tensile (breaking) strength at Day 14 showed no treatment-related differences.'}, {'topic': 'Pharmacokinetics and bioanalysis', 'summary': 'Plasma LT3114 concentrations were quantitated by two ELISA methods (human IgG direct-binding and antigen-laid down/binding ELISA); all treated animals had measurable concentrations and the two assays yielded generally similar results, but no clear dose-proportional increase was observed between 10 and 50 mg/kg; detailed numeric results are provided in the pharmacokinetic report and data tables.'}, {'topic': 'Safety, clinical observations and data integrity', 'summary': 'All animals survived to scheduled termination with no compound-related clinical findings and no meaningful body weight effects; a protocol deviation (postdose observation timing on Day 4) was recorded and judged not to affect interpretation of the study.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'This report describes a human tissue cross‑reactivity study performed to evaluate potential off‑target binding of LT3114‑CF, a humanized anti‑LPA monoclonal IgG1 (κ), on cryosections of normal human tissues. An indirect immunoperoxidase immunohistochemistry method was applied to a panel of 38 human tissues (per Annex II guidance) from ≥3 donors (except breast and parathyroid, n=2) at two concentrations (1 and 10 µg/mL) with appropriate positive (LPA[C12]-SMCC-BSA) and negative (S1P-SMCC-BSA) spot controls and assay/isotype controls; tissue adequacy was validated by anti‑vimentin staining. LT3114‑CF stained the positive control intensely and produced no LT3114‑CF–specific staining in any human tissue evaluated; the isotype control did not show specific reactivity. Runs with inadequate positive control staining (Runs 1 and 16) required restaining of affected tissues. The study was conducted under Alizée Pathology SOPs with documented GLP exceptions (method development pilot unaudited, analytical testing of final dilutions not performed as specified) and no statistical analysis was performed due to the semiquantitative data.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study objective and scope', 'summary': 'Evaluate potential tissue cross‑reactivity of LT3114‑CF on normal human cryosections as part of preclinical safety assessment, following recommendations in Annex II (Directive 75/318/EEC) and FDA CBER guidance.'}, {'topic': 'Test articles and controls', 'summary': 'Test article LT3114‑CF (humanized IgG1 κ anti‑LPA, CF‑conjugated) and isotype control LT1023‑CF were used; positive control was LPA(C12)-SMCC-BSA spot and negative control S1P‑SMCC‑BSA; assay control used diluent only.'}, {'topic': 'Methods and assay conditions', 'summary': 'Indirect immunoperoxidase IHC on 4–5 µm acetone/NBF‑fixed cryosections; primary at 1 and 10 µg/mL (selected from pilot validation), mouse anti‑FITC secondary, Dako EnVision+ HRP polymer and Sigma Fast DAB detection; tissue validation by anti‑vimentin.'}, {'topic': 'Tissues, donors and data handling', 'summary': 'A panel of 38 normal human tissues from at least three donors was evaluated (breast and parathyroid had only two donors available); staining was scored semiquantitatively for intensity and frequency and recorded in tabulated microscopic data (Appendix A).'}, {'topic': 'Results, conclusions and quality considerations', 'summary': 'Positive control stained intensely confirming assay performance; LT3114‑CF showed no specific binding to any evaluated human tissues and no unexpected reactivity was observed. Some runs (1 and 16) had inadequate positive control staining and affected slides were restained. The report documents GLP‑related exceptions for the pilot method development and for analytical testing of final dilutions; no statistical analysis was performed due to semiquantitative data.'}]}

summary.summary: {'summary': 'Study DGG14-010 evaluated tissue cross-reactivity of LT3114-CF (a CF-conjugated humanized IgG1 κ anti-LPA antibody) on cryosections of normal human tissues. LT3114-CF and CF-conjugated isotype control LT1023-CF were applied at 1 and 10 µg/mL to cryosections from a panel of 38 human tissues (generally from ≥3 donors) using an indirect immunoperoxidase method with anti-FITC secondary and Dako EnVision+ HRP detection. Positive (LPA[C12]-SMCC-BSA) and negative (S1P-SMCC-BSA) spot controls and anti-vimentin tissue validation were used; two runs had inadequate positive control staining (Runs 1 and 16) and affected slides were restained. summary.summary: {'summary': 'A 14‑day C57BL/6 mouse wound‑healing study evaluated LT3114 given subcutaneously (0, 10, 50 mg/kg; n=8 females/group) on Days 1, 4, 8 and 11. LT3114 at both 10 and 50 mg/kg produced significantly accelerated wound closure versus vehicle (10 mg/kg p < 0.0006; 50 mg/kg p < 0.0101) but did not alter tensile strength of healed wounds (terminal tensile strength in the normal range, 9.37–10.86 g/mm2). All animals survived with no compound‑related clinical findings or body weight changes. Plasma LT3114 was quantifiable in all animals by two ELISA methods (direct human IgG and antigen‑laid down binding ELISA); the assays gave generally similar results but no clear dose response was observed between 10 and 50 mg/kg. A single protocol deviation (Day 4 1‑hour postdose observation recorded ~2 hours postdose) was reported and judged not to affect study interpretation.', 'topics': [{'topic': 'Study design and procedures', 'summary': 'C57BL/6 female mice (8/group) received SC doses of LT3114 (0, 10, 50 mg/kg) on Days 1, 4, 8 and 11 following two wound types created on Day 1 (6 mm cranial punch and 1 cm caudal linear incision). Cranial wounds were used for percent wound closure and terminal tensile strength; photographs were taken on Days 1, 3, 6, 9, 13 and terminal and body weights recorded pre‑surgery and on Days 7 and 13. Analgesia (0.05 mg/kg buprenorphine) and standard wound dressings were applied; terminal blood was collected by cardiac puncture for plasma analysis.'}, {'topic': 'Efficacy outcomes', 'summary': 'LT3114 significantly accelerated wound closure at both 10 mg/kg (p < 0.0006) and 50 mg/kg (p < 0.0101) versus vehicle, with similar healing profiles between the two doses (no significant difference between doses, p < 0.2526). Area under the percent‑closure/time curve (AUC) was used to summarize healing over time. Despite accelerated closure, tensile strength at Day 14 was unchanged across groups and remained within the reported normal range (9.37–10.86 g/mm2).'}, {'topic': 'Pharmacokinetics and bioanalysis', 'summary': 'Terminal plasma LT3114 concentrations were measurable in all animals using two complementing ELISA methods (direct human IgG quantification and antigen laid‑down binding ELISA). The two methods produced generally similar values; however, no clear dose‑proportional increase in plasma levels was observed between the 10 and 50 mg/kg groups. Detailed individual concentration data and assay methods are provided in the Pharmacokinetic contributor report.'}, {'topic': 'Safety and tolerability', 'summary': 'All animals survived to scheduled termination with no compound‑related clinical signs or meaningful body weight changes. A few incidental dorsal skin abrasions were observed across groups and were not considered treatment‑related. A single protocol deviation (late postdose observation on Day 4) was reported but not considered to affect study integrity or conclusions.'}, {'topic': 'Statistics and data handling', 'summary': 'Percent wound closure and tensile strength were analyzed using one‑factor ANOVA with trend and Dunnett’s test where applicable; AUC for wound closure was calculated by the trapezoidal rule (% closure × days).
